Nevertheless, these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks designed to deceive predictions. This paper introduces PointClipber, the initial framework capable of simultaneously and individually attacking points within volumetric subregions of a point cloud. Unlike prior methods that attack isolated points or entire subregions, PointClipber grants an adversary fine-grained control over every point, allowing independent decision-making for each. This capability enables the attack space to expand to any vertex within a 3D bounding box. PointClipber utilizes these diverse attack spaces to expand the search domain and discover novel adversarial points. The framework's effectiveness is validated through comparative analysis with state-of-the-art single-point attack methods and by demonstrating currently unattainable attack configurations via attack landscape visualization. To address the high computational cost of attacking individual points, we propose a training-free reconstruction approach that achieves nearly identical prediction dropouts with significantly reduced computation. We release PointClipber to facilitate future security research and provide an interface in the AOPC library, which supports various point cloud formats and includes a visualization module for attack analysis. Neural network-based point cloud models are now widely adopted in practical applications and are critical to safety-critical systems like autonomous vehicle Lidar detectors. Consequently, these systems remain a focal point for adversarial attacks. However, existing attacks either target single points or the entire cloud, limiting the attack space to discrete points. This restriction reduces the search space for optimizing adversarial perturbations and may fail to attack points that do not originally require modification. To solve this, we introduce PointWise, a novel attack paradigm that treats each point in the cloud as an independent attack target, offering fine-grained control over all points simultaneously. This approach drastically expands the attack space, making it impossible for traditional grid-search-based defense mechanisms to cover it completely. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PointWise by achieving a 99.99% prediction dropout rate on the NVIDIA Ventho vehicle point cloud when attacking a network trained without noise. This approach successfully located poles corresponding to RPA excited states, including the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. While the giant resonance is traditionally characterized as a single state with significant strength and width, the RPA analysis reveals that it actually consists of multiple distinct poles. The findings indicate that poles linked to RPA excited states are directly observable through experimental width measurements. In many of these contexts, the underlying systems are dynamic, and due to their inherent complexity, constructing mathematical models suitable for clustering techniques is often unfeasible. Furthermore, existing methodologies frequently fail to account for the stochastic and noisy nature of the data. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel, general, and straightforward mathematical framework designed to detect communities in both time-series and simultaneous data. This approach utilizes a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (GHMM) as its foundational framework. The proposed method involves fitting a GHMM to the data to identify associated communities, followed by a transformation of the GHMM parameters into a visible structure. The effectiveness of this community detection strategy is validated through various numerical experiments, including a case study on a simultaneous stock market dataset and a time-series case study using noisy sensor data from a rotating disk. Ultimately, the findings demonstrate that the proposed method yields distinct and meaningful communities in both data types, whereas traditional clustering algorithms are unable to achieve this result. Additionally, the paper presents a tutorial on the underlying mathematical models and a discussion of potential future applications. The key contribution of this work is a mathematical model for hidden structures that effectively detects communities in noisy, high-dimensional time-series and simultaneous data, a capability that current standard clustering methods do not possess. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/PeimanJalali/Community_Detection. The findings indicate that the proposed method can identify significant communities in financial and scientific datasets that other techniques cannot find, and it is also effective with noisy sensor data from potentially interesting physical systems. Consequently, researchers can apply this method to their own datasets to explore for communities that were previously undetectable.

To evaluate the detectability of this phenomenon, we constructed a mathematical model incorporating key variables such as microbial survival duration, stellar velocity dispersion, and ejecta dispersion. Our analysis indicates that the statistical pair-distribution function, representing correlations between life-bearing systems, could serve as a viable diagnostic tool for interstellar panspermia, specifically when ejecta velocity dispersion exceeds stellar dispersion. By offering heuristic estimates of model parameters across different astrophysical settings, we conclude that open and globular clusters are the most promising environments for testing the feasibility of interstellar panspermia. A parallel key area in wildlife science involves estimating and modeling population density and size. While recently developed spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models achieve this goal by combining individual encounter histories with auxiliary spatial data on capture locations, they have not yet been extended to explicitly model space usage and resource selection. These SCR models incorporate encounter probability functions that are conceptually similar to RSFs, yet existing frameworks lack the capability for joint inference on these specific ecological processes.

This study introduces a statistical framework for simultaneously modeling space usage, resource selection, and population density. This approach integrates SCR data—such as that from camera traps, mist-nets, or conventional catch-traps—with resource selection data gathered from telemetered individuals. The proposed method relies on marginal likelihood estimation to concurrently determine parameters for both SCR and RSF models.

The results indicate that this integrated method enhances the precision of population density estimates and improves parameter estimation for standard SCR models. Crucially, the findings demonstrate that SCR models alone cannot estimate resource selection function parameters; these must be estimated jointly. Furthermore, the results show that biased population density estimates can arise if resource selection is modeled separately rather than included as part of the overall encounter probability function.

Although developed initially for marked individuals, this approach can be adapted for unmarked individuals. The proposed framework is general and can be extended to incorporate complex SCR scenarios, including correlated movements, hierarchical models, and spatially explicit population models. By enabling simultaneous inference on multiple significant ecological processes, this framework offers a more robust and precise method for estimating population density and selecting primary research tools for specific applications. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jeremychandler/SCR_SRS.

to program testing, with the goal of enhancing the reliability of software development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing serves as the specification for a testing environment, which functions as the final stage of a toolchain designed to assist professional developers, hobbyists, and computer science students. This environment features an automated algorithm that identifies errors within executed tests and guides their correction by displaying a stick diagram of causal execution chains on a screen. Users can navigate this diagram backward, similar to using a satnav to follow roads on a map, which highlights the specific locations in the code that require modification to eliminate the error. We have released the environment's implementation alongside a library of formal algorithms, including an executive for tracing executions, a translator for converting specifications into execution traces, and a validator for analyzing those traces. The environment's success in an evaluation demonstrates its utility: executed tests either fail immediately or pass without triggering any error alarms, and when new requirements are added, the automated algorithm efficiently finds a minimal execution trace that exposes the missing behavior. Furthermore, the implementation of the backward algorithm Dijkstra's K-shortest paths algorithm ensures the environment operates with maximum efficiency by having low space complexity, handling long execution traces without excessive memory consumption. Additionally, the environment can be utilized to execute standard unit tests, although it offers superior reliability by automatically locating and highlighting errors in the tests themselves. Since its launch in 2015, the environment has been integrated into educational settings, where its visual feedback has been shown to help students understand the execution of algorithms and data structures. Looking ahead, the environment can be employed to increase the reliability of test suites, provide feedback during the drafting of specifications, and enhance the instructional value of assignments involving test execution and specification creation. The environment is available for others to use in ensuring the reliability of their own code or in educational contexts.

a sparse network of unknown dimensions, even when compromised by a significant number of Byzantine actors. We operate within the full information model, wherein Byzantine nodes possess complete awareness of the network's state at every step—including all random choices—unlimited computational capabilities, and the freedom to deviate arbitrarily from the protocol. Our primary contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm capable of estimating network size despite a high volume of Byzantine nodes. Specifically, this algorithm accurately estimates the size of sparse, small-world expander networks containing up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ represents the unknown network size and $\delta$ is any fixed positive constant. The algorithm produces a constant-factor estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability, ensuring that a large majority ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction) of honest nodes obtain the correct network size. Furthermore, the approach is fully distributed, lightweight, and easy to implement; it completes in $O(\log^3{n})$ rounds, utilizes small messages per round, and imposes minimal local computational costs on each node. It is important to note that achieving accurate size estimation in anonymous, sparse networks without the aid of unique identifiers is extremely challenging. Our solution overcomes this by employing a "growing forest" mechanism to accurately count nodes in expanders through accurate sampling. This mechanism is universally applicable to any sparse small-world expander network. Prior to this research, the exact network size could only be determined in fully connected anonymous networks free of Byzantine nodes. In such expanders, Byzantine nodes may adopt various strategies, including mimicking multiple legitimate nodes, masquerading as such, or behaving erratically. In contrast to previous literature, we do not seek to determine the polylogarithmic-accurate size of network $n$; rather, our goal is to enable the majority of nodes to accurately ascertain that their network size is $X$. We assume an asynchronous environment with message delays and failures, allowing Byzantine nodes to completely ignore the protocol. The proposed solution relies on the assumption of a bounded diameter bound, denoted as ${\sf DBN}$, which exceeds the actual network diameter (${\sf DBN} > n^{1-\delta}$). We also explore the feasibility of accurate size estimation in power-law networks in the subsequent paragraph. We propose a novel approach rooted in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Unlike conventional methods that treat the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation for a specified mean curvature $K$, our method solves an algebraic equation for $K$ given a chosen conformal factor. This strategy circumvents the challenges regarding the existence and uniqueness of Hamiltonian constraint solutions without resorting to the standard rescaling of source terms, a feature that is critical when sources are fundamental fields, as reconstructing their configurations from rescaled data can be problematic. Employing an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this technique yields rapidly convergent solutions for several previously unexplored initial conditions in numerical relativity: specifically, (i) periodic inhomogeneous spacetimes featuring large random Gaussian scalar field perturbations, and (ii) asymptotically flat black hole spacetimes containing rotating scalar clouds. Numerical results confirm that this method produces six-dimensional conformal scalar curvature $R^\ast$ that satisfy the Hamiltonian constraint to an extremely high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, these findings align perfectly with results obtained using the standard CTT constraint damping method. Crucially, this approach requires solving only one additional linear PDE—governing the conformal factor $\psi$—compared to the standard constraint damping procedure. We emphasize that this method is directly applicable to numerous other standard CTT constraint damping schemes. These findings significantly strengthen the robustness of current numerical relativity efforts investigating fundamental physics, such as black hole rotation and scalar self-interaction, and can be readily utilized in studies involving periodic boundary conditions, including those exploring gravitational waves from binary mergers, dark matter interactions around rotating black holes, and instability analyses of compact objects. Numerical data and computational codes utilizing this method will be made publicly available.

Antiferromagnetic antiperovskites represent an emerging class of materials that display diverse properties driven by their intricate electronic band structures and magnetic ordering. However, reports on the anomalous Nernst effect and its magnitude within this specific class remain scarce, a limitation likely attributed to the experimental challenges in accurately determining the anomalous Nernst coefficient. In this study, we present experiments on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic antiperovskite thin films. By utilizing the same sample and measurement geometry for both the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects, we enable a direct comparison between these phenomena to precisely quantify the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermoelectric anomalous conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN shares a similar origin with its anomalous Hall conductivity, rooted in the band structure and spin arrangement characteristic of the three-sublattice antiferromagnetic state. We also examine the temperature dependence of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and discuss how spin-orbit scattering influences its sign and magnitude. These findings offer insights into the potential for engineering the anomalous Nernst coefficient through chemical substitution in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites. This coefficient can facilitate the creation of transverse voltage gradients from longitudinal temperature gradients in antiferromagnetic devices, thereby facilitating thermoelectric signal propagation across magnetic domain walls and into semiconducting leads. The results derived from Mn$_3$NiN serve as a foundational reference for future efforts aimed at optimizing the anomalous Nernst coefficient in this material system. Recent advancements in automation and experimental methodologies have accelerated these measurements and enhanced their resolution, resulting in massive datasets requiring analysis. These improvements are especially notable at user facilities and synchrotron light sources. Although machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly utilized to process and interpret large data volumes in real time, significant hurdles remain: the general user community often lacks ML expertise, and deploying ML models presents technical challenges. In this work, we showcase several representative ML models designed for on-the-fly analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II). We provide an instructive overview of these examples, emphasizing the integration of models into current experimental workflows to enable readers to incorporate their own ML strategies at NSLS-II or similar facilities. The proposed framework demonstrates that with minimal effort, diverse ML models can function alongside feedback loops by leveraging the existing Bluesky Suite for experimental orchestration and data management. While this example is rooted in NSLS-II, the framework is designed to be facility-agnostic, allowing for the sharing of simple and complex ML models among users who can integrate experiments using the versatile Bluesky platform. The featured ML models range from basic techniques like principal component analysis and single-crystal Rietveld analysis to advanced approaches, including a neural network for cubic zirconia phase identification and a model for orienting rhombohedral lithium niobian crystals. This framework is open to further expansion, and we encourage the community to contribute models for phases such as high-temperature superconductors or for characterizing properties like anisotropy, symmetry breaking, domain structures, chiral phases, or topological features. All presented models and the framework are available for download, and we invite feedback and suggestions for improvement. Ultimately, we aim to facilitate a user-friendly environment where general users can experiment with multiple ML models simultaneously to analyze imaging data from multiaxis goniometers or other imaging setups.

The integrand $f$ satisfies $p$-growth conditions with respect to the gradient, where $1<p<2$. Specifically, we demonstrate that when the obstacle $\psi$ is bounded, a Sobolev regularity condition on the gradient of $\psi$ implies the same regularity for the gradient of the solution, assuming the partial derivative map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ resides in the Sobolev space $W^{1, p+2}$. This work introduces novelty by addressing subquadratic growth conditions, characterized by $f(x, \xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ with $1<p<2$, where the coefficient function $a$ is itself a member of a Sobolev space. Our findings imply that both the solution and the gradient exhibit regularity equivalent to that of the obstacle and the coefficients, provided the exponent $q$ in $W^{1,q}$ satisfies $q>pq$. We note that while the optimal regularity corresponds to $q=\infty$, our results hold for any $q>pq$. These conclusions are validated through numerical examples. iller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable composites to "see" their own complex damage mechanisms with high accuracy. Beyond through-holes and delaminations, this enhanced self-sensing capability may eventually allow materials to detect and report even more intricate damages, such as cracks or tears. We believe this advancement will significantly strengthen the monitoring and maintenance systems for laminated composites across various industrial applications. The results from this study are presented in two parts: first, the introduction of the technique and its validation, and second, the accurate reconstruction of multiple through-holes in CNF-reinforced GFRP laminates, followed by a comprehensive analysis of source localization errors and the factors influencing them.

The vast diversity of life has resulted in a wide array of locomotive designs and methods, with various creatures utilizing legs, wings, fins, and other mechanisms to traverse their environments. This report defines the movement of general biological species as biolocomotion and introduces a computational method to identify it within raw video footage. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, dense, invertible, underdetermined, or overdetermined. Empirical results across various scenarios demonstrate the NN method's superiority, with improvements of up to one order magnitude in convergence rate, computational complexity, complexity per successful iteration, and overall complexity, as determined by the intersection of sparse complexity and RAM constraints. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. Numerical experiments are also presented. Contextual linear bandits were previously contextualized for distributed solutions where agents could access contexts in \cite{ashkenazi2020distributed} and \cite{goulart2019distributed}. Our work, however, tackles a more challenging context where agents are unable to transmit their observed contexts to the learner. We prove that an agent only requires $\approx 5d$ bits of randomness to select a report that helps the learner achieve optimal performance. This compression rate represents a negligible overhead compared to prior methods \cite{goulart2019distributed}, which could not access contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this compression rate is information-theoretically optimal. The agents' ability to compress contexts into such short representations without degrading learner performance beyond logarithmic regret factors is valuable in itself. Methods addressing context compression in other application areas are discussed in \cite{eliar2020context} and \cite{dwork2010fair}. Context selection relates to dimensionality reduction techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and embedding methods, which aim to represent high-dimensional data compactly to facilitate efficient storage, retrieval, and computation; see \cite{le2013semantic} for an overview. Related research includes dimensionality reduction for classification and regression (e.g., \cite{daskalakis2021dimensionality}, \cite{candès2018robust}, \cite{eliar2020context}), which typically assumes access to context distributions.

F) analyses and extremal network theory, this research investigates the maximum performance improvement of optimal power control compared to binary (on/off) strategies within large-scale interference networks to derive novel theoretical insights. Although numerical evidence suggests that binary power control is nearly optimal in most practical scenarios, this extremal analysis reveals that significant gains from optimal control can exist in specific settings, while also establishing GDoF-based bounds for these maximum gains. The study's primary contribution is the explicit characterization of the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control as $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ for any number of users $K$. Specifically, this gain is bounded between $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and $2.5\sqrt{K}$. For networks with $K=2,3,4,5,6$ users, the exact extremal gains are determined to be $1, 3/2, 2, 9/4$, and $41/16$, respectively. Networks achieving these extremal gains can be viewed as multi-tier heterogeneous systems. It is important to note that since the focus is on asymptotic analysis, these sharp characterizations of extremal gains hold primarily theoretical value and do not contradict the established understanding that binary power control remains generally close to optimal in practical, non-asymptotic environments. Additionally, this paper provides the first explicit example where the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control exceeds $1$. Finally, we examine the impact of mobility, or "random walk" user behaviors, on these extremal gains and demonstrate that such mobility can reduce the extremal gain down to a constant value of $1$. This result implies that in many mobile communication scenarios, optimal power control offers at most a factor of $C$ improvement (where $C$ is a constant) over binary power control, reinforcing the feasibility of implementing binary control in practical systems. These findings and their associated examples are entirely theoretical; they do not negate the prevalence of green networks utilizing on/off power control in practice, nor do they preclude the potential for future reductions in the constant $C$. The implications of this work extend beyond its direct applications in extremal network theory, offering valuable perspectives for engineers designing future mobile networks. The explicit example of extremal gain $41/16$ presented here represents a significant improvement upon the previous best bound of $9/4$.

The MTSA is readily implementable in current particle-resolved simulation frameworks, such as for the particle interaction module in OpenFOAM. We urge researchers to adopt this efficient and accurate approach to model particle collisions in their simulations.

terrain remains a difficult and unresolved challenge in robo-physics, as the uncertainty arising from ground deformation hinders both dynamical modeling and control strategies. Furthermore, determining efficient and stable movement mechanisms on soft ground presents a significant hurdle. This study aims to control a one-dimensional monopod hopper to achieve a target jump height. To accomplish this, I first established and validated a discrete element method (DEM) simulation environment featuring spherical granular material as the soft ground. Using this setup, I developed ground reaction force models based on resistive force theory (RFT). These RFT models were then employed to create a feedforward force control system for the robot. Within the DEM simulation, a feedback control loop was implemented to correct deviations between the actual ground reaction forces and the RFT predictions. Consequently, the robot successfully tracked desired trajectories and reached the target height within five hops, significantly reducing apex position errors compared to using feedforward control alone. Additionally, the experiment varied the robot's square foot area from 1cm² to 49cm². The results demonstrate that the feedback controller effectively manages fluctuations in ground reaction forces, even when the foot dimensions are comparable to the size of individual grains. However, control challenges increase as the foot area grows larger. Although this research focuses on a specific task (monopod hopping) and a particular type of deformable terrain (granular media), the approach of combining RFT with feedback control offers a potential framework for controlling legged robots on various soft grounds. Future work should explore more complex locomotion tasks, such as crawling or jumping without initial velocity, on natural and complex soft terrains. To achieve this, accurate ground reaction force models for those environments and scalable feedback controllers are essential. Ultimately, this research contributes to the automation of apex height tracking in single-leg hoppers over granular media by integrating RFT and feedback control.

While numerous statistical and computational models exist for automatically generating these hierarchies, current methods often fail to account for the linkages inherent in information networks, which are ubiquitous in real-world contexts. Additionally, existing approaches typically represent topics as abstract probability distributions over words rather than as concrete nodes derived from the original network, and the statistical techniques employed in prior works often lack the capacity to process data at Web-scale. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), which leverages a distributed vertex-programming process to compute a nonparametric Bayesian generative model. Experimental results on three medium-sized datasets and the complete Wikipedia dataset demonstrate that HDTM is capable of inferring accurate hierarchies even when applied to large-scale information networks. Furthermore, the proposed approach represents one of the few capable of operating effectively on datasets as large as Wikipedia. Beyond HDTM, this work also introduces several novel methodologies and metrics for the automatic evaluation of learned hierarchies. Experimental findings indicate that HDTM surpasses baseline models in almost all assessed metrics across various datasets. The proposed method offers several advantages over prior approaches: (i) it produces compact, high-quality hierarchies even when applied to large-scale datasets, (ii) it utilizes the original network structure to derive concrete topic nodes, and (iii) it employs a flexible nonparametric Bayesian framework. Documents are intrinsically linked, yet standard topic models often ignore this fact because they treat input data as independent terms or topics. We introduce the Linked Topic Model (LTM), a framework designed to incorporate intrinsic linkages into a parametric generative model. LTM utilizes the frequency of mutual links between documents to estimate a shared distribution of latent topics per document. By conditioning on a neighbor's topic distribution, the model captures the influence of document linkages. Experiments on three datasets with known underlying structures show that LTM effectively integrates these structures and reconstructs them more accurately than baseline models. Specifically, the linkages of apriori clustered topics in LTM align significantly closer to the true structure of Instagram captions compared to other models. Furthermore, models incorporating linkages tend to generate semantically similar neighboring topics. Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum quantum gap squared—can be recovered through a linear quench of a single time-independent parameter that characterizes the annealing path. We analyze both random Hamiltonians and specific instances of the transverse-field Ising model on one- and two-dimensional lattices. For the latter, we perform exact calculations and show that, in the large system size limit, the quenched estimates of the gap squared for both random instances and the frustrated Ising model align closely with their annealed counterparts. Additionally, we compare our findings with recent results from the Los Alamos National Laboratory. While a random quench of Ising parameters generally yields higher gap squared values than an abrupt quench to a fixed final state, there are cases where the random quench fails to capture the true ground state energy density. These failures arise when the random quench produces a Hamiltonian with a gap squared significantly smaller than that of the original instance, causing the post-quench decoherence time to exceed the thermal relaxation time. Such scenarios indicate that the annealing algorithm has identified a local minimum trap. We also investigate the optimal quench speed, noting that while there is no strict upper bound, excessively fast quenches can result in inaccurate gap squared estimates. Our findings suggest that, for system sizes relevant to current experiments, the linear quench protocol offers a robust method for estimating the minimum quantum gap squared. These estimates can help determine whether a quantum annealer has found the exact ground state energy density or merely a local minimum, an issue particularly pertinent to identifying the ground state of frustrated systems. Furthermore, our approach can estimate the decoherence time of a quench, accounting for both environmental noise and finite quench speed. This suggests that experimental estimates of the quantum gap squared need not be orders of magnitude larger than the system's actual value to remain accurate. Our proposed simple quench protocol may thus enable more precise estimates of the quantum gap squared in future experiments. However, it is important to recognize that these estimates remain approximate, as they rely on the single parameter $\beta$, an assumption of infinite quench speed, and finite system sizes. Despite these limitations, the protocol represents only a minor modification to the standard quench

two-band model for infinite-layered nickelates, derived from $d$ and $s$-like orbitals, can be mapped onto a single-band Hubbard model, identifying the screening of the more itinerant $s$-band as a critical factor. Without screening, a strongly correlated band yields an antiferromagnetic ground state. Under weak screening, strong correlations drive electrons out of the $s$-band, resulting in an undoped Mott insulator with half-filled $d$ orbitals; this scenario contrasts with high-$T_c$ cuprate observations and suggests $s$-wave pairing for the superconducting state. Conversely, strong screening leads to partially filled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands that couple weakly, resembling a self-doped $d$ band with tendencies toward $d$-wave pairing. Specifically, in the strong screening regime, mapping to a one-band model reveals interesting spectral weight transfers when the $s$-band is partially occupied, indicating effective long-range attractions for electrons within the $d$ band—first observed in doped single-band models around $x \sim 0.19$. Consequently, both scenarios can produce high-$T_c$ physics previously seen in cuprates, provided the $s$ and $d$ bands are strongly coupled and the ratio $U/t$ is close to 10. Finally, we outline simple experimental tests, such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and $k$-resolved spectral weight analysis, to determine whether the electronic structure of infinite-layer nickelates corresponds to a one-band $d$ physics model or which of the two other scenarios applies. We also briefly extend this analysis to other square-lattice materials, including $Y_{1-x}Ba_{x}NiO_{4}$, $\ce{La2NiO4}$, and $\ce{Sr2NiO3}$, and compare findings with existing experimental data. ARPES results for Yb- and Ho-doped $\ce{La2NiO4}$ show good agreement with both the weak and strong screening scenarios, implying that structural parameters alone cannot predict the number of active bands; instead, the degree of $s$-band correlation must be determined experimentally for each specific material. This work provides a theoretical framework to guide future experiments and extract parameters for effective one-band models from multi-band nickelates.

As density rises in compact stars, the sound velocity is anticipated to approach the conformal limit ($c_s/c=1/\sqrt{3}$) at high densities while adhering to the causality constraint ($c_s/c<1$), yet its precise behavior continues to be a subject of intense debate. It has been proposed that the sound velocity serves as a key indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, implying a specific functional form for its density dependence. This study investigates the general characteristics of the sound velocity and adiabatic index across hybrid stars, neutron stars, and quark stars, employing various conditions for the hadron-quark phase transition with differing interface tensions. Our findings indicate that the anticipated sound velocity behavior can also arise from the nonperturbative properties of the quark phase, independent of a deconfinement transition, resulting in more compact stars with comparable masses. Consequently, we introduce a novel class of quark star equations of state that could be validated by future high-precision radius measurements of pulsar-like objects. Specifically, the parameter $\Delta=c_s^{max}/c_s<1.7$, which quantifies the variation of the sound velocity, correlates directly with the star's compactness and is linked to the ratio between surface and bag pressures of quark stars. Moreover, the final properties of these quark stars are strongly influenced by the phase transition properties at nuclear saturation density, which are dictated by the competition among the bag pressure, strong interaction attraction, and relativistic effects within the quark matter. We conclude that the sound velocity and adiabatic index can yield valuable insights into the internal composition, physical conditions, and the nature of the phase transition for quark stars.

We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Furthermore, assuming additional compactness of the level set curves, we conclude that all harmonic functions with two ends are constant. These findings extend previous work by Cadidus and Vezzoni. Additionally, we show that two gradient shrinking Ricci solitons with the same dimension and constant scalar curvature are isometric. This result improves upon established literature by confirming that any two such solitons are isometric when they share the same gradient norm at a single point. This compactness condition aligns with general principles: harmonic functions on complete manifolds that are both bounded and exhibit polynomial growth are necessarily constant. Our paper contributes to this area by asserting that functions with polynomial growth that are also convex are constant. These compactness conditions are crucial for establishing that harmonic functions on Einstein manifolds with positive scalar curvature are constant, a conclusion first reached by Yang and Qian. However, it is important to note that our approach does not depend on the minimal distortion method employed by Yang and Qian. Our proof strategy involves defining a Riemannian manifold composed of connected components of level set curves, then constructing a measure on this manifold to create a harmonic function. The core of our argument consists of analyzing the restrictions of the original harmonic function and the potential function of the Ricci soliton to the Riemannian manifolds, ultimately showing that a convex harmonic function with two ends is constant. This paper aligns with research by Baras and Li, as well as Yang and Qian, in exploring the link between the geometry of manifolds and the properties of harmonic functions, utilizing the compactness of level set curves rather than the minimal distortion method. Our results also relate to studies by Ammann,et al. regarding Einstein manifolds and Einstein metrics, particularly concerning the existence of metrics with prescribed scalar curvature isometric to a given manifold. We hope that our techniques regarding isometric Einstein metrics and the correspondence between isometric manifolds with different Einstein constants will assist in classifying gradient shrinking Ricci solitons with constant scalar curvature. Additionally, our findings are applicable to determining when solutions to the Einstein constraint equations on manifolds with boundary are constant, a problem investigated by Anderson, Chen and Zhang, and Yang and Zhang. a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice. Consequently, we introduce a straightforward modification to the model architecture that enables these attacks to function effectively. This finding serves as a cautionary note against the premature adoption of dynamic backdoor detection methods during the development of defensive strategies. The proposed attack code will be released after the fact check concludes.

light propagation models grounded in the parametrised post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework designed to test potential deviations from general relativity. Among these effects, the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which quantifies gravitational light deflection, significantly influences astrometric data. This study analytically and numerically investigates how deviations of $\gamma$ from its general relativity value of unity impact parallax measurements in Gaia-like systems. Analytical calculations determined the changes in observable quantities resulting from minor variations in PPN $\gamma$, while numerical simulations were conducted to verify how these observable shifts translate into parallax estimation errors. The results indicate that a deviation in $\gamma$ causes a global parallax shift; a corresponding formula for this bias was derived, incorporating the satellite's barycentric distance, the angle between the spin axis and the Sun, and the uncertainty in $\gamma$. Numerical simulations of astrometric solutions corroborate these theoretical findings. Current estimates of PPN $\gamma$ suggest that the contribution to the Gaia parallax zero point is unlikely to exceed 0.2 $\mu$as. Furthermore, simulations reveal a strong dependence of the parallax shift on ecliptic latitude, an effect attributed to an asymmetry in the Gaia scanning law. This conclusion is fully supported by additional simulations utilizing a reversed precession direction for the spin axis relative to the Sun. We also examine the determination of parallax as a free parameter versus its fixation to zero and the impact of maskings, such as those caused by bright stars. Ultimately, given the high precision of modern parallax estimates, relativistic phenomena can no longer be neglected. Consequently, we recommend incorporating the latest PPN $\gamma$ estimates into data reduction pipelines for astrometric satellites and provide methodologies for estimating the resulting parallax shifts.

answering questions requiring commonsense background is common practice, yet it risks introducing noise and misleading data due to the vastness of available information. To address the challenge of effectively integrating relevant knowledge, we introduce a semantic-driven, knowledge-aware Question Answering framework that regulates knowledge injection through a coarse-to-fine approach. This framework employs a tailoring strategy to filter extracted knowledge based on the coarse semantics of the query during the extraction phase. Additionally, we developed a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that leverages structural knowledge to hierarchically fuse appropriate information according to the fine-grained semantics of the questions. Experimental results on the CommonsenseQA dataset show that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches. Furthermore, a case study was conducted to illustrate the regulatory effect of our framework on both extracted knowledge and candidate answers. The source code for this paper is available at https://github.com/yanjiazheng/semantic-aware-knowledge-qa.

Question answering is fundamental to human intelligence, involving not only language comprehension but also world knowledge reasoning. We present a coarse-to-fine semantic-driven Question Answering framework that regulates external knowledge to enhance answer fusion accuracy. Unlike existing methods that randomly extract knowledge, our approach uses semantic similarity for coarse filtering to reduce noise. Additionally, we introduced a hierarchical knowledge retrieval module based on structural relationships that adaptively fuses fine-grained knowledge. Experimental results on the CommonsenseQA dataset indicate that our method surpasses baseline models. A case study further demonstrates the framework's ability to tailor extracted knowledge and improve answer fusion. The code is open-source at https://github.com/yanjiazheng/semantic-aware-knowledge-qa.

Question answering is pivotal to human intelligence, requiring not only language comprehension but also the reasoning of external knowledge. Experiments on the CommonsenseQA dataset show that our approach outperforms baseline models. These cations generally exhibit brighter electronic emissions at longer wavelengths compared to their neutral counterparts. A comprehensive grasp of their near-UV to visible characteristics would enable their use as probes for local plasma conditions or as tracers for neutral gas within cometary systems. However, constructing complete spectral models for small, oxygen-containing molecular cations remains unfeasible due to current limitations in available molecular data. While the five simplest species—H₂O⁺, CO₂⁺, CO⁺, OH⁺, and O₂⁺—are well-characterized in certain spectral regions, they lack robust reference data in others. These knowledge gaps impede the creation of fully quantitative models of cometary spectra, specifically hindering accurate assessments of physical-chemical processes derived from the most common cometary molecules. This work compiles existing spectral data for these species and identifies critical areas requiring future research, particularly where data scarcity significantly limits our understanding of cometary evolution. By leveraging the VCOMA virtual laboratory, this analysis gathers and organizes references into a structured database, facilitating easier access to current knowledge and streamlining the collection of data for future theoretical studies. Consequently, this compilation and the associated database serve as essential foundations for constructing comprehensive spectral models of key cometary species, which would offer profound insights into the physics and chemistry of cometary atmospheres and tails.

A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models. To investigate the impact of data heterogeneity, we establish two distinct statistical models. First, we consider pairwise exchangeable data and derive an exact asymptotic analysis of the bias and variance of the resulting "local update" algorithms. This model captures moderate data heterogeneity, such as classification tasks where class proportions vary between nodes. Second, to address more general multi-class exchangeable data, we employ the Delta Method to obtain asymptotic expressions for bias and variance. We also examine non-exchangeable data as a special case. These findings establish lower bounds on communication compression that prevent model divergence. Building on this foundation, we propose an iterative algorithm to minimize bias variance trade-offs, thereby extending the acceptable range of communication compression without causing model divergence. Our results indicate that communication compression levels up to $O(1/N)$ are permissible, which aligns with and extends prior bounds established in classical (centralized) statistics for exchangeable data. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings using a synthetic dataset and an image classification task on MNIST. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art approaches, including standard FL, drop-out techniques, and bias-reduction methods designed for heterogeneous data. This study represents the initial attempt to utilize exchangeable data theory to analyze bias and variance under data heterogeneity, to define corresponding thresholds, and to develop optimizing algorithms. The core theoretical contributions generalize exchangeable data frameworks to accommodate significant data heterogeneity. Unlike previous approaches that rely on i.i.d. assumptions and heuristic derivations (often limited to two classes) that frequently lack closed-form solutions, our framework is broad, rigorous, and produces explicit results. These generalizations were necessitated by real-world applications where node data is typically neither i.i.d. nor exchangeable. We acknowledge that these findings are also relevant to "map/reduce" learning on distributed databases. Crucially, the proposed framework establishes tighter bounds for bias variance trade-offs in "local update" algorithms compared to existing literature on exchangeable data, as it avoids the Cramer-Wald bound lower bounds often found in FL papers. The key innovation of this work is framing data heterogeneity as a statistical model to achieve these improved bounds.

This method employs a consistency regularization strategy that integrates adversarial training with a diversity-based constraint. The consistency loss is defined as the difference between predictions from two networks trained on distinct regimes: one using only hard-labeled samples and the other using labeled samples selected via a labeling oracle that prioritizes hardness and distribution diversity. While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and rigorous evaluation of these methods remains difficult. First, existing data preprocessing steps are often proprietary and custom-tailored, hindering experimental standardization. Second, current DLKT studies frequently employ inconsistent evaluation protocols that lack alignment with real-world educational settings. To resolve these issues, we present \textsc{pyKT}, a comprehensive Python-based benchmark platform designed to ensure valid comparisons across DLKT methods through exhaustive evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library features standardized, integrated preprocessing procedures for seven popular datasets across three distinct evaluation paradigms. Our empirical analysis within this framework reveals several key findings: first, comparing DLKT methods is challenging due to varying preprocessing approaches, and second, the FET score emerges as the most reliable metric for KT performance. Additionally, our results challenge recent claims regarding the superior effectiveness of attention mechanisms and transformers in DLKT contexts. To advance future research, we also propose several guidelines for evaluating DLKT methods. Finally, we plan to utilize the \textsc{pyKT} benchmark to investigate novel topics, such as the impact of incorrect answer handling and the transferability of DLKT models. We have open-sourced \textsc{pyKT} alongside documentation and tutorials that facilitate comparing DLKT methods and conducting exploratory research, particularly in areas like curriculum learning and knowledge graph integration.

SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed in various applications, and other solvers also produce proofs using this standard. To inform future enhancements, we seek community feedback. In this process, we examine the format's history, outline our pragmatic development strategy, and address potential issues that may emerge when other solvers utilize the format. We particularly focus on backward compatibility, as adding solver-specific features risks breaking parsers used by proof validation tools for other solvers. We propose addressing this challenge in a modular fashion. Ultimately, we invite others to use this approach to develop a parser and validate proofs generated by other solvers. The source code for this parser is accessible here: https://github.com/ThomasSchaefer/parasol. The format is officially documented at https://github.com/parasol/parasol-format. We also provide examples of proof objects, their parsing, and validation at https://github.com/parasol/parasol-format/tree/main/examples. Our goal is for this page to serve as a living document, with examples gradually added to cover a broader range of scenarios. The proposed format is backward compatible with versions from 2009 to 2013. The official website is located at https://people.cs.univie.ac.at/schaefer/veriT/. The parasol-format is licensed under GPL v3. We appreciate any feedback regarding bugs, limitations, or suggestions for improving both the format and its parser, which can be posted on the veriT GitHub page or sent to Thomas.Schaefer@univie.ac.at. Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, we achieved a WER of 19.5% using a model trained in just four hours on a hybrid system composed of an English pre-trained model, an intermediate model, and a Czech model. Comparisons with other transfer strategies and ablation studies on the intermediate model highlight the efficacy of the intermediate alphabet approach over other common methods like character-level sharing or acoustic feature sharing. Additionally, an analysis of acoustically similar sub-words reveals that the intermediate model successfully aligns sub-words across different languages. All source code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/eva-machova/ASR-transfer.

Neural machine translation (NMT) has seen rapid adoption, yet it demands extensive in-domain data and computing resources. Transfer learning is increasingly recognized as a solution, even across related but distinct languages. This paper investigates the transfer of a multilingual NMT system from English to a low-resource setting by integrating a German model into an English-based system. We compare two transfer methods: one utilizing shared acoustic features and another using character-level embedding sharing. Results indicate that both approaches significantly outperform standard NMT on the target language and achieve comparable performance to each other. The shared acoustic feature method was implemented using a acoustic tower trained on concatenated English and German features, whereas the character-level method was applied to encoder embeddings. These findings confirm that cross-lingual transfer enhances NMT efficiency, particularly in low-resource scenarios. An open-source implementation of the proposed methods is available at https://github.com/zeyuazh/NMTransfer.

This paper reframes distinct GEC domains as separate tasks and introduces a meta-learning framework for few-shot domain adaptation that requires no pseudo data. By leveraging data-rich source domains, we learn model parameter initializations that enable rapid adaptation to new, resource-constrained target domains. Specifically, we adapt the GEC model to the first language (L1) of second-language learners. Our evaluation utilizes a source domain from the L2 Arabic First Language Acquisition (L1A) corpus and three target domains, including a newly released L1A corpus and two other L1A datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot GEC domain adaptation techniques. Furthermore, our approach surpasses data-driven zero-shot domain adaptation methods that use a total of 20 times more training data than the combined L1A sources. The core contribution of this work is the utilization of first-language data for GEC domain adaptation, addressing a scenario with extremely limited source and target domain resources. To validate our framework's effectiveness, we assembled and released a high-quality L1A corpus, offering approximately 5,000 sentences of second-language learners' data in L1A. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/MohamedOmar666/L1A-GEC. Indices and terms are accessible at https://ojs.academicjournalcenter.com/index.php/AJCE/article/view/5063. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing an affirmative answer. We analyze two algorithms recognized for generating such allocations in non-strategic environments: Round-Robin, which yields EF1 allocations for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method by Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM Journal of Discrete Mathematics, 2020] that produces EFX allocations for two agents. We demonstrate that all pure Nash equilibria of Round-Robin result in allocations that are EF1 relative to the agents' true values. Furthermore, we show that the Plaut and Roughgarden algorithm not only achieves EFX but also satisfies maximin share fairness in this strategic setting—a property it does not possess in the non-strategic case. Additionally, we prove that a weaker version of this result applies to any two-agent mechanism that consistently yields pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations. We conclude by discussing mechanisms for multi-agent environments that always yield EFX allocations.

839 exhibits almost no star formation, except for a prominent complex of HII regions situated at the very edge of its outer disc. To investigate the origins and characteristics of this feature, researchers compared new Hα and archival broad-band imaging of UGC 8839 with similar data from four comparable spiral galaxies. The findings suggest that the star formation in UGC 8839's extreme outer disc is not a highlighter effect resulting from the concentration of long-period orbits near apogalactiocenters. Instead, it likely stems from a distinct population of dark matter-subdominant satellites driving local over-densities in the halo. UGC 8839 stands as the only galaxy where this specific star formation mechanism can be directly observed. Furthermore, this population may account for the excess of baryons and the flattened rotation curves frequently seen in local spiral galaxies. UGC 8839 thus offers significant potential for studying these phenomena and testing theoretical models regarding the outer disc formation and evolution of spirals. The event driving the enhanced star formation is not a super-starburst, nor is it linked to a merger or interacting companion; rather, it represents the first identified instance of enhanced star formation so far from the disc centre in a non-interacting spiral galaxy. This suggests that the extended star formation processes in spiral galaxies remain poorly understood. UGC 8839 serves as a prime example of a galaxy that requires high-resolution, deep imaging to uncover the often-subtle events responsible for its outer disc formation.

While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha and discuss their implications for population studies of classical T Tauri stars. Comparing mass accretion rates derived from fitting UV-to-near-infrared spectra in recent X-Shooter observations with those measured 11 years prior using the same instrument, we find that XX Cha exhibits nearly 2 dex of accretion variability between 2010 and 2021. While the specific timescales of this variation remain uncertain, XX Cha demonstrates extreme accretion variability for a classical T Tauri star. If such behavior is common among these stars, potentially occurring on timescales longer than previously investigated, it could significantly influence disk evolution models constrained by the observed spread in accretion rates. Finally, we note that earlier studies relying on spectral lines to assess accretion variability may have underestimated the fluctuations in certain targets.

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Evaluations across discrete control environments (StarCraft II and multi-agent particle environments) and continuous control settings (multi-agent MuJoCo) demonstrate that our method yields significantly superior results on complex, mixed offline multi-agent datasets, particularly when there are substantial disparities in the quality of individual trajectories. Furthermore, we release our code and dataset at this address to promote further research. Experimental analyses confirm that the proposed framework yields marked performance gains over current SOTA methods when facing mixed offline multi-agent datasets, yet shows negligible advantage over the SIR framework when individual trajectories are randomly sampled, effectively validating the design of our approach. Finally, we also present an extension of the SIT framework to handle online partial observability. Code for both SIT and e-SIT is available at this link. Benchmark results indicate that our method surpasss SOTA approaches on mixed offline multi-agent datasets across all three tested environments.

conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance"—triggered by measurement. This event preceded the famous Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen critique. In this work, we utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous nonlocal nature of wave function collapse, combined with single-particle entanglement, generates the nonlocal effect known as steering. During this process, Bob's quantum state becomes contingent upon the specific observable Alice chooses to measure. To achieve this, we fully harness the spatial spreading of the single-particle's entangled wave function over large distances. Specifically, we show that the nonlocality inherent in single-particle entanglement enables the particle to "know" which detector Alice employs to steer Bob's state. Consequently, despite significant counterarguments, we establish that single-particle entanglement produces genuine nonlocal effects across distant locations, thereby opening avenues for implementing truly nonlocal tasks using this phenomenon. Ultimately, we highlight that while single-particle entanglement is inherently nonlocal, its practical utility is constrained by the limited size of the entangled wave function and the necessity that the detector's location lie within this region. These findings reveal that the magnitude of single-particle entanglement's nonlocal effects varies continuously from zero up to the full scale of standard quantum mechanics, depending on the relative positioning of the source, detectors, and the particles they measure. This underscores that single-particle entanglement constitutes a progressively stronger form of nonlocality, ranging from negligible to maximally so. We conclude by outlining potential applications of single-particle entanglement in communication and computation, such as enabling communication without classical channels and facilitating remotely shared quantum gate operations. These outcomes underscore that single-particle entangrance is both a progressively stronger type of nonlocality and a resource capable of achieving nonlocal tasks that are impossible with separable states. These findings emphasize that the nonlocality of single-particle entanglement is a physical reality, not merely an artifact of first-person measurement or statistical ensembles, and that the limitations on its wave function's spatial extent are solely practical. These results also provide a framework for evaluating the degree of nonlocality in single-particle entangled states and offer a methodology for experimenting with nonlocality in laboratory settings. advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with evolving IoV architectures. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for enhancing data privacy and security within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant potential through its secure, decentralized, and auditable mechanisms for data recording and sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application and implementation of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. Additionally, it examines potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research directions associated with these frameworks. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for developing modern Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions to address various data privacy issues and scenarios in IoVs. To contextualize the survey, the authors begin by introducing the basics of IoVs, FL, and Blockchain technologies, followed by a detailed examination of Blockchain-Enabled FL frameworks, their implementation processes, and key design considerations such as data auditing, model updating, secure parameter sharing, and efficient framework design. Finally, the survey concludes with a discussion on KPIs for evaluating FL framework performance, along with challenges, research gaps, and potential future directions. Indices / Terms: Internet of Vehicles, Federated Learning, Blockchain Technology, Data Privacy and Security, Cryptocurrency.

Early spectral data indicate multiple, interacting mass ejections, with shocks from these events driving both the initial optical brightness and gamma-ray emission. The system entered solar conjunction shortly after the eruption; upon re-emergence, the nova had transitioned into the nebular phase, revealing the tail end of the super-soft X-ray stage. Later optical observations tracked the fading ejecta and a persistent narrow-line emission spectrum originating from the accretion disk. Continued hard X-ray emission suggests a standing accretion shock within an intermediate polar. Optical analysis determined an orbital period of 3.230 $\pm$ 0.003 days, with no detected white dwarf spin period. Data derived from light curves, spectral evolution, and multi-wavelength observations across the eruption cycle were used to determine the mass of the white dwarf ($M_{WD}$) and the system's ejecta mass ($M_{ej}$). The measured $M_{WD}$ ranges from 0.86 to 1.16 $M_{\odot}$, depending on the assumed mass transfer efficiency, while $M_{ej}$ is estimated at $0.15 \pm 0.02 M_{\odot}$. Post-nova observations showed the system had temporarily exited the main dwarf nova outburst cycle before restarting it approximately one year later. V392 Per's properties suggest it may reside near the dwarf/intermediate polar classification boundary and could serve as a potential dwarf nova recurrent nova hybrid. Following the eruption, V392 Per spent over three years evolving into its nebular phase, providing exceptional insights into the connection between dwarf novae and novae. This study offers extensive observational data on the event and presents a comprehensive analysis of the nova's various evolutionary stages.

During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed signal to calculate the responsibility of each GMM component. The feedback transmitted to the BS comprises the index of the component with the highest responsibility, allowing the BS to select the corresponding codebook entry. Simulation results indicate that this proposed design and feedback scheme surpass conventional Lloyd clustering-based algorithms, particularly in scenarios with reduced pilot overhead. Furthermore, the approach offers a flexible and general design principle that accommodates various codebook generation and feedback encoding strategies. Specifically, by employing an extended GMM with truncated higher-order moments, the method achieves a second-order adaptive design for UL data transmission. Consequently, the algorithm by reference [1] is recovered when a single component is assigned to the mean of this extended GMM. Furthermore, by utilizing K components for the responsibility feedback, the algorithm from [2] is replicated. The proposed design also extends to joint clustering of UL and downlink (DL) training data, as well as the integration of delay-Doppler domain information. We note that the core algorithm is straightforward to implement and can be readily adapted to create content-based codebooks for cognitive radio communications.

We present a framework to achieve these currents on a cubic three-dimensional (3D) lattice featuring a Hofstadter model connected to two heat baths at distinct temperatures. Our results demonstrate that these currents possess dissipative robustness, maintaining stability despite impurities and gauge field tilting within specific nonequilibrium states. Furthermore, we identify protected boundary currents with authentic 3D robustness, meaning their stability relies on tunnelling occurring across all three spatial dimensions. The model also supports generic surface currents that remain robust in both bosonic and fermionic systems. Since the introduction of the Bernoulli effect and the Magnus force, the interplay between geometry and dynamics has remained a vibrant area of research. This work explores such mechanisms within a tightly controlled quantum system defined by a two-dimensional (2D) Heisenberg antiferromagnet subjected to orbital fields. We observe that adiabatic cycles in the time-evolution Hamiltonian induce nonzero Chern numbers and topological terms in effective Landau-Lifshitz dynamics for the magnetic order parameter. These topological terms give rise to dissipative Magnus terms in the equations of motion for magnons, thereby establishing topological magnon bands. We provide explicit examples of orbital fields and driving protocols that generate Chern bands, accompanied by illustrations of their experimental detection. Additionally, we examine the robustness of these effects, the scalability of this approach to higher dimensions, and the efficiency of low-dimensional approximations. The phenomena described represent a novel class of effects, as they demonstrate the emergence of band structure and topological characteristics in the quasiparticle excitations of a continuously excited, inherently topological many-body system.

Excitations with nontrivial topological charges can emerge in nonequilibrium quantum systems driven by external fields. We investigate this phenomenon in a spin chain featuring a specific pattern of magnetic bonds. By employing a bosonized approach, we establish the topological charge of magnons and demonstrate its robustness across arbitrary dimensions and interactions. Within Einstein gravity, the sufficient condition for this implies an upper bound on the Bondi mass $m$, specifically $|\dot{m}|\leqslant 0.3820~c^3/G$, offering a novel viewpoint on Dyson's maximum luminosity. Conversely, in Brans-Dicke theory, the sufficient condition relies on the scalar radiation field's behavior; photons can reach null infinity provided the scalar gravitational radiation remains moderate and the rate of mass loss is not excessive. These results are directly applicable to binary black hole mergers involving masses comparable to those of stellar-mass or larger compact objects. The derived general results are supplemented by explicit examples of static spacetimes in both theories. In particular, we examine the generalization of the Levi-Wiltschko type II (1969) solution for Brans-Dicke theory and demonstrate that such solutions allow light from finite distances to reach null infinity only when the coupling constant exceeds $4\pi$. These findings advance our understanding of whether radiation from astrophysical sources can be observed by distant observers across various scalar-vector-tensor theories of gravity. We have extended these analyses to encompass radiation from infinitesimal sources, including massless and massive scalar-field radiation, as well as radiation from point particles in Brans-Dicke theory.

We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as cosmic structures develop, calculating how field stars' dynamical friction drives these remnants into NSCs. Subsequent evolution inside the clusters is modeled through three-body interactions and gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Our results indicate that 7.5% of Pop III binary remnants will migrate to the galactic centers (within 3 pc). Of these, approximately 5–50% will merge at redshifts greater than zero within NSCs, a process that includes systems with initially large separations (up to 1 pc). The merger rate density (MRD) reaches its peak at $z\sim 5-7$, ranging from $\sim 0.4-10\ \rm yr^{-1}\ \rm Gpc^{-3}$, which translates to a potential detection rate of $\sim 170-2700\ \rm yr^{-1}$ for third-generation GW detectors capable of observing up to $z\sim 10$. The majority ($\gtrsim 90\%$) of these mergers occur in low-mass ($\lesssim 10^{6}\ \rm M_{\odot}$) NSCs formed at high redshifts ($z\gtrsim 4$). While GW observatories will determine the masses of these Pop III binaries, their formation channels remain uncertain; thus, placing observational limits on the MRD is crucial for constraining these unknowns. These remnants may also produce fast transients distinct from massive Pop III single-star mergers, potentially explaining some RATS. Furthermore, the MRD in existing galactic NSCs is roughly 2.5 times higher than previously reported literature values, suggesting an accelerated timescale for the first merger in the Milky Way's center.
