Initially, the study focuses on a single-user, single-relay configuration, addressing a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay under individual power constraints for both nodes, with the goal of maximizing the end-to-end secrecy rate through optimal power allocation across sub-carriers. Subsequently, the research expands to a more complex multi-user, multi-relay scenario. Utilizing a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximation for the end-to-end secrecy rate, an optimization problem is defined to jointly optimize power allocation at the base station, relay selection, sub-carrier assignment to users, and power loading at each relay node. The objective is to enhance overall system security while adhering to independent power budget limits at each transmitter and exclusive sub-carrier allocation constraints inherent to OFDMA. A joint optimization solution is derived using duality theory, where dual decomposition enables the application of convex optimization techniques to determine power loading at source and relay nodes. Additionally, the paper examines an optimization for relay power loading, relay selection, and sub-carrier assignment given a fixed base station power allocation. Finally, a sub-optimal scheme exploring joint power allocation across all transmitting nodes with fixed sub-carrier and relay assignments is analyzed. Simulation results are provided to validate the performance of the proposed schemes. Distinct from existing literature, this work applies a high SNR end-to-end secrecy rate approximation suitable for multi-hop networks to a practical PLS problem involving OFDMA, a multi-user framework, and independent power constraints at source and relay nodes—a scenario未曾被 explored in current research. Consequently, a convex optimization problem is formulated for relay power loading, and optimal power allocation strategies are determined for the base station and sub-carriers assigned to relays using Lagrangian duality. For the remaining problems of base station power allocation and relay sub-carrier assignment (with fixed power loading), optimal solutions are derived via dual decomposition, followed by simulations demonstrating the performance gains of the proposed schemes. Additionally, an optimization problem is formulated for a single-carrier multi-relay network to compare performance against the OFDMA-based multi-relay scheme; this problem is solved optimally using sequential convex optimization (SCO), and simulation outcomes illustrate the results.

However, existing systems are hindered by slow performance, limited to roughly 300 steps per second, primarily because of outdated infrastructure. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance framework implementing three standard text game benchmarks that boosts simulation speed by a factor of 1,000, achieving more than one million steps per second on standard desktops. This dramatic improvement drastically cuts experiment duration, allowing researchers to conduct billion-step simulations within a single day. Because the primary application space for text-based games is large-scale reinforcement learning, we evaluated TextWorldExpress at every stage of the learning pipeline—policy gradient, value based, and model based—using state-of-the-art algorithms. Our results demonstrate that a successful policy can now be trained from scratch using billion-step counts within a week. Furthermore, we provide access to text world experiments conducting trillions of environments per second. To facilitate this, TextWorldExpress offers 3x speedups over current benchmarks across all task types, including free text generation, scripted commands, and regular expressions. Additionally, it delivers an order-of-magnitude improvement in performance for multi-step reasoning experiments. Beyond standard benchmarks, the framework supports custom games, enabling users to define any text-based simulation in under 20 lines of code. The source code is released openly to encourage further advancements in artificial intelligence. Experiments confirm the method's efficiency, surpassing one million steps per second. TextWorldExpress represents a substantial leap forward in text-based experimentation, offering an extensive speedup over prior methods, and simultaneously advances the field of text-based game creation. The framework is available at https://github.com/aminehassoun/textworldexpress.

TextWorld is a text-based adventure platform built to help researchers evaluate natural language understanding in artificial agents. While valuable for experimental work, its current implementation is a performance bottleneck. This lack of speed restricts the scale of learning experiments, forces compromises on dataset size or complexity, and hinders the use of state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods. We present a Python library designed to accelerate simulation in TextWorld games by three orders of magnitude. This improvement enables large-scale experiments, such as training a billion steps with a specific model over the course of a week. Additionally, the library allows for the rapid creation of custom text-based experiments; for instance, training agents to solve specific puzzles in non-deterministic text worlds can now be completed in minutes. a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in training and inference times, along with significant energy savings. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor network FDHT models, our FDHT-LSTM achieves higher accuracy across all tested image and video classification datasets with even greater efficiency. The FDHT-LSTM model (1.8MB) outperforms the PyTorch implementation (14.5GB) by more than an order of magnitude in both training and inference speed while reducing energy consumption by over 50\times. Yet, current assessments and policy guidance on market design and ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interactions between markets and services. To address this gap, this paper introduces an open-source agent-based model designed to evaluate design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA toolbox for power system analysis. A stylized simulation scenario was used to validate the model and explore a specific redispatch design issue. The findings regarding multi-period all-or-none order types in redispatch markets reveal three key implications: (1) The order design minimizes risk for market participants by ensuring full order clearance. (2) Large orders can create dispatch ramps before and after delivery periods, potentially triggering ramp-risk mark-ups and increasing intra-day imbalance risks for missing trades. (3) In continuous trading periods, the all-or-none design may lead to clustering of start and finish times, causing redispatch to occur simultaneously with generation from other activated units. This study constrains the formation and dissipation timescales for vortices in both hemispheres, focusing on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), characterized by higher temperatures and increased hydrocarbon levels at millibar pressures. While the NPSV began forming in late northern spring, it lacked the distinct thermal and compositional contrasts observed at the south pole during its southern summer by the end of Cassini's observations, shortly after the northern summer solstice. The newly formed NPSV was defined by a steepening thermal gradient near $78^\circ$N. Its hexagonal boundary suggests that the Rossby wave responsible for Saturn's persistent polar hexagon—previously thought to remain in the troposphere—can impact stratospheric temperatures roughly 300 km above the cloud tops. We speculate that this hexagon may serve as an anchor, organizing the NPSV's shape and regulating its growth and decay, a hypothesis that could be tested with future Saturn observations. In the southern hemisphere, the NPSV initiated in mid-southern spring, reached its peak intensity at the southern solstice, and persisted until late southern summer. Its poleward-moving maximum exhibited a distinct trajectory, and the two polar jets associated with the NPSV were the most robust seen at Saturn to date. These findings enhance our understanding of the NPSV's complex evolution at Jupiter and the two polar jets at Uranus and Neptune, offering insights into how these systems influence atmospheric chemistry and thermal structures across the outer planets. By the mid-1980s, following the foundational work of Deligne and Langlands on local constants for geometric measures on conjugacy orbits, the focus had shifted toward more technical investigations into how these measures behave under L-functions, automorphic forms, and the Langlands correspondence. However, a renewed interest in Beyond Endoscopy—pioneered by Altug—is prompting a deeper, more detailed examination of these same measures. This shift is necessary to advance current understandings of L-functions, automorphic forms, and the Langlands correspondence, particularly in efforts to define and analyze "new forms," which represent generalized levels or critical points of L-functions. While modern analyses often employ relative Chebotarev theorems, exploiting shared information in powers of Frobenius elements at potentially the same prime to reduce analytic thresholds for error estimates, an alternative strategy involves minimizing analytic errors by precisely matching the scales of these primes. This latter approach requires a rigorous understanding of the geometric measures on conjugacy orbits that underpin these reductions. Although such a project would ultimately aim to establish effective versions of the Langlands correspondence, this note has more modest objectives: to introduce some fundamental concepts and calculations regarding measures on these orbits. Although an informal, illustrative, and somewhat repetitive style has been used to explain examples from both the general theory and the specific case of $\mathrm{GL}_2$, this work serves as a resource of references, definitions, and computational details regarding measures on algebraic tori that may facilitate future endeavors to directly link new automorphic forms with new L-functions.

Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. Nevertheless, phase information is often critical for reconstructing target details, a principle established in coherent x-ray imaging. This work presents a novel phase retrieval algorithm capable of recovering field phase data from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra. We demonstrate this technique using x-ray scattering from Mössbauer nuclei at a synchrotron facility. Access to phase data enables a superior reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental results—a level of precision unattainable through conventional methods. Consequently, our approach offers a powerful new tool for data analysis that will advance both x-ray quantum optics and synchrotron-based Mössbauer spectroscopy. Ultimately, achieving x-ray quantum optics requires controlling light at the single-photon level, a prerequisite for advancing quantum imaging, communication, and computation with atoms and nuclei. While significant progress has been made in generating such single x-ray photons, deterministic single-x-ray sources remain absent. We propose a futuristic concept for determining the energy spectrum of quasi-monochromatic x-ray quantum states generated via coherent scattering from Mössbauer nuclei. This scenario, feasible at next-generation light sources, employs an interferometric x-ray quantum microscope for spectrum determination that relies solely on intensity measurements, as there is no phase screening in x-ray quantum optics. Furthermore, we provide estimates of required experimental parameters, which are identified as realistically achievable. Ultimately, this paper outlines a path toward producing and measuring single-x-ray photons from a laboratory source.

Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. It contains roughly 2000 sentences, each annotated with its associated semantic relation and the predicted plausible discourse marker. We also present a range of analyses based on this dataset that reveal complex interactions between markers and relations, leading to refined characterizations of markers across different contexts. Since the definition of a discourse marker relies on its expected relationship with subsequent discourse, we discuss the applicability of our characterization to markers defined within monosentential contexts. DiscSense represents the first comprehensive, bottom-up characterization of discourse markers based on their relations to the information conveyed in sentences. By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood around local minimizers. Our proofs rely on a detailed landscape analysis of a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, serving as a pivotal intermediate step. Additionally, our conclusions rest on a standalone result identifying that the geodesic ball centered at $Y$ with a radius equal to one-third of $Y$'s least singular value forms a geodesically convex set under the Riemannian quotient norm.

Our introduced "social-learning" variants successfully establish this equilibrium, whereas "individual learning" versions fail to converge strategies to the Nash outcome. When players utilize "canonical co-evolutionary genetic algorithms," the game dynamics form an ergodic Markov Chain; consequently, we analyze simulation results using both specific methodologies and broader statistical tests. These analyses reveal that in the "social" scenario, states corresponding to Nash Equilibrium play are highly frequent within the chain's stationary distribution, while in the "individual learning" scenario, the equilibrium is never reached. Furthermore, the expected Hamming distance between limiting distribution states and the "NE state" is markedly smaller in the "social" case than in the "individual learning" case. We also estimate the time required for "social" algorithms to reach the "NE state," verify their robustness, and demonstrate that a substantial proportion of played games indeed occur at the Nash Equilibrium. The findings indicate that the game constitutes an effective mechanism for fostering the formation of a "collective intelligence" capable of solving for the Nash Equilibrium in the Cournot game. These results align with prior research showing that such algorithms enable genetic algorithms to develop a "collective learning" capacity to reach the Nash Equilibrium. This work contributes by offering detailed quantitative analysis of how these algorithms drive genetic processes toward equilibrium, revealing that the "NE state" is not only rapidly accessed but also represents a dominant component of the system's long-term behavior. Additional findings include a numerical lower bound for the proportion of games played at the Nash Equilibrium and a detailed examination of the distribution of Hamming distances from the "NE state." Additionally, we observe that as population size $n$ increases, the proportion of games played at the NE state initially rises before declining, and that increasing tournament length $T$ significantly boosts the probability of reaching the Nash Equilibrium. The implications of these results are discussed in light of previous studies on genetic algorithms, complexity theory, and statistical physics. To ensure reliability in real-world deployments, these systems must remain robust against hardware soft errors that corrupt platform memory. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier CNNs by showing that range supervision acts as a highly dependable fault detector and mitigator for relevant bit flips, specifically within an eight-exponent floating-point format. Additionally, we investigate novel, non-uniform range restriction techniques that successfully reduce the likelihood of silent data corruptions and uncorrectable errors. As a practical, safety-critical end-to-end demonstration, we apply our method to a vehicle classification task using ResNet-50 and the MIOVision traffic camera dataset. The quantitative results presented here can serve as a foundation for developing further, potentially more sophisticated, safety arguments for CNNs. Consequently, this paper demonstrates how to leverage formal methods to construct robust safety cases for deep learning systems. Notably, our approach is directly applicable to other safety standards, such as ISO/IEC 26262 for the automotive sector. To facilitate this, we openly release the relevant analysis tools and scripts. Our formal method ensures the efficiency of the safety argument by rigorously verifying the precision of key quantitative metrics, such as the probability of undetected bit flips, the mean time to undetected failure (MTUD), and the partial fault coverage (PFC) for the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, we utilize the zTest to establish statistical confidence in our findings. The formal verification of the entire safety argument was conducted using the model checker NuSMV. Finally, we ensure that all assumed preconditions and intermediate claims, including the partial fault coverage of relevant errors, are also formally verified. The proposed methodology can be adapted to similarly assess the safety of other CNNs, including those executed on embedded deep learning processors like the DA850. Those adaptations would primarily involve updating the relevant data structures and algorithmic steps. We emphasize that this work adopts a bottom-up, structural approach to safety argumentation, which is the recommended methodology for achieving certified safety cases for software systems. This ensures that all necessary safety properties are explicitly defined and verified. Our formal technique for building such safety cases is uniquely valuable because it guarantees the mathematical precision of all intermediate and final claims within the argument.

. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. Additionally, comparisons with internal attention models highlight the significance of using external memory at different attention heads for integrating visual and inertial data. The source code for our model is accessible at: https://github.com/zixiangzheng/VIO-MA.

These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories. Our findings indicate that while the increase in both entropy and temperature—mandated by the Clausius inequality of classical thermodynamics—is necessary to avoid violating the QNEC in quenches involving transitions between thermal states with momentum (dual to BTZ geometries), it is not sufficient. For any arbitrary initial state, we establish lower and upper bounds on the increase of entropy (or temperature) given a fixed increase in temperature (or entropy). These results provide concrete examples of quantum lower and upper bounds on irreversible entropy production, confirming their existence as previously theorized. Additionally, we observe a monotonic behavior in the non-saturation of the QNEC over time following a quench and analytically derive their asymptotic values. Our study demonstrates that the entanglement entropy of an interval of length $l$ consistently thermalizes within time $l/2$ with an exponent of $3/2$. Furthermore, we analytically determine the coefficient of the initial quadratic growth of entanglement for any $l$ and show that the slope of the linear growth of entropy after the quantum information theory (QIT) phase transition is determined by the coefficient of the universal finite term of the CFT central charge. Our analysis reveals that the coefficient of the initial quadratic growth of entropy is universally connected to the CFT central charge, the length of the entangled interval, and the temperature of the dual thermal state in the low-temperature limit. These analytical results align with previous numerical findings. Ultimately, the paper reinforces that the violation of the QNEC in quantum systems serves as a robust criterion for analyzing dynamical processes in quantum field theory.

The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on modeling and observations, we outline plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus from accretion to its present state. Three specific scenarios are highlighted: first, desiccation caused by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase; second, a prolonged period of surface liquid water followed by climate destabilization and a runaway greenhouse effect; and third, inefficient outgassing that retained water within the planet, trapping hydrogen in the core and oxidizing the mantle. Finally, we discuss current evidence and the future observations and missions needed to refine our understanding of Venus's history and the intricate feedback cycles operating among its interior, surface, and atmosphere across past, present, and future timescales.

This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. The application of this technique to other problems within various CFT$_{2}$s constitutes a promising direction for future research. Consequently, if the conformal weight and spin of a primary are known, its OPE block can now be efficiently computed, thereby enabling the rapid determination of scaling dimensions and spins for long primary states via the bootstrap approach. On SIMD accelerators like GPUs, this limitation stems primarily from memory allocation and access issues. Although a few libraries offer parallel memory allocation for accelerator devices, they all suffer from uncoalesced memory accesses.

We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over individual kernel latency.

To optimize data access, our SoA layout stores all object fields related to an iterator (an index into an array of objects) in contiguous memory. Consequently, data access becomes coalesced, and we replace sequential iftests with efficient, fully parallel all operations.

We evaluated DynaSOAr using nine C++ benchmarks representing different application categories. The results demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves up to an order of magnitude better performance than sequential execution and matches the performance of carefully hand-tuned GPU kernels. Furthermore, our memory allocator reduces global memory fragmentation by up to an order of magnitude compared to other dynamic allocators. DynaSOAr also exhibits excellent scalability, handling both fixed and growing numbers of objects, and shows excellent portability, successfully running on both GPU and CPU architectures.

DynaSOAr thus allows programmers to write highly parallel, single-method, multiple-object applications in Python without sacrificing performance. In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. Our primary tool is a novel relative version of theis theorem, which establishes that groups with polynomial diameter possess many conjugacy classes of small size; this result generalizes work by Breuillard, Guralnick, and Mazur to the context of group extensions. As an additional finding, we prove that the typical element in such groups is conjugate to an element of the large abelian section. Furthermore, we provide applications regarding groups possessing a high number of conjugacy classes and characterize groups with polynomial diameter when group rings are considered. Finally, we note that all results remain valid if the requirement for a large abelian section is replaced by having a large sectional zero width.

Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this mass accretion. The implications of this finding for the relationship between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function require further investigation. Additionally, the core mass spectrum in the G28.37 region does not align with predictions derived from the Jeans mass using the observed density and temperature distributions. This suggests that either the uncertainties in these core properties are substantial or that gravity is not the primary force determining the mass scale across the entire spectrum. Alternatively, magnetic fields or turbulence could be dominant; however, analyzing the observed fraction of magnetized cores indicates that magnetic fields are unlikely to be the primary driver in this specific sample. Instead, turbulence may be responsible for this deviation. Ultimately, the formation of massive stars cannot be understood solely through collapse and fragmentation mechanisms; in the G28.37 region, the available mass in cores appears insufficient to account for all observed protostars, implying that massive stars likely form within larger, fragmented structures whose properties differ significantly from those of dense cores. This study underscores the necessity of future surveys with improved sensitivity to both mass and size to better characterize the origin of massive stars.

Specifically, for the sphere ${\mathbb S}^{d-1} \subset {\mathbb R}^d$, the strict positive definiteness of a zonal function $f(\cos \theta)$ is governed by the signs of the coefficients in its expansion using Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$, where $\lambda=(d-2)/2$. While recent findings indicate that classical differentiation and integration preserve positive definiteness in this setting, these operations shift the space dimension in increments of two. This paper introduces operators for zonal functions on the sphere that maintain (strict) positive definiteness while transitioning between dimensions by steps of one. These fractional operators are specifically designed to act suitably on the Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$. Notably, a method to maintain positive definiteness across dimensions for spherical functions was previously established only for the Fourier transform on ${\mathbb R}^d$. The proposed fractional operators generalize as follows: $\sqrt{I-\Delta_{\mathbb S} }$ corresponds to the standard Zemlyakov transform, and $\frac{1}{r} {\mathbb E} \left( \sqrt{1-T^2_{d } } \right)$ to the spherical Fourier transform. Furthermore, we establish that the operator $I-\Delta_{\mathbb S}$ is strictly positive definite, potentially offering a novel approach to proving the positive definiteness of functions on the sphere. The paper also features a appendix containing MATLAB code implementing these fractional operators on zonal functions, alongside numerical experiments illustrating applications in strict positive definiteness and spline interpolation. Our results extend the research of Schecar and Stelestan on similar topics regarding zonal functions. Recurrence relations for special functions frequently yield operators capable of operating within the same dimension; however, this work demonstrates a mechanism to facilitate transitions across different dimensions. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has seen widespread adoption, with the attention mechanism being a central component of state-of-the-art models. Despite this, the standard attention mechanism remains limited in capturing long-term dependencies within source sentences. This paper introduces two hierarchical cross-domain attention mechanisms designed to model these long-range dependencies by leveraging target words from other sentences. Specifically, we propose intra-corpus cross-domain attention (IC-CA) for introducing model parameters derived from within the same corpus, and inter-corpus cross-domain attention (ICIC-CA) for integrating parameters from a different corpus. We conduct experiments on machine translation between English and Chinese news and web domains. Results show that adding IC-CA achieves an average of 0.51 BLEU points improvement over the base NMT model, while combining both mechanisms yields an 0.81 BLEU point gain. These findings indicate that hierarchical cross-domain attention mechanisms effectively address long-term source dependency issues and are beneficial for machine translation. In this expression, $\phi(x,b) = \mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$, where the parameter $\kappa(x,b)$ is given by $\frac{\sqrt{1-x} b - \sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x} b + \sqrt{1+x}}$. The coefficient $b=b_S \geq 0$ quantifies the asymptotic asymmetry between positive and negative excursions of the walk, taking the value $b_s=1$ when the increments are symmetric. This result generalizes the classical $\sqrt{1-x}$ behavior observed in symmetric random walks ($b=1$) and encompasses the limit of highly asymmetric walks, yielding exponent $\phi(x,b)=1-\sqrt{1-x}$ so that $p(t,x) \sim (3-t)/2$ for $t<3$. The derivation accounts (as do existing literature) not only the emergence of the $\phi(x,b)/2$ exponent from the branching process approximation of the walk but also the precise determination of $\phi(x,b)$ through its relationship with the branching process's local time at zero. Furthermore, the computation of $b$ from the increment distribution is framed as an optimal stopping problem, with its continuity and monotonicity w.r.t $x$ established via coupling. Numerical simulations are presented to illustrate these findings. The approach also elucidates why, for any fixed $x<1$, the averaged fraction of non-negative time asymptotically follows a $\text{Beta}(1,1)$ distribution conditioned on exceeding $x$ when $b=1$, and explain how these averages relate to the exponent $\phi(x,b)$. (IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 0.1 meters in length and 0.4 meters in diameter, generates the required plasma environment ahead of the ICRF antenna. This source, which features a helical antenna, was engineered to achieve a helicon discharge mode. Although it was previously unconfirmed whether the source could reach this mode, achieving helicon operation is crucial for maximizing the source's capacity and producing high-density plasma. Consequently, a comprehensive study was conducted to attain helicon mode. This involved characterizing key plasma parameters—such as electron temperature, density, and plasma potential—and implementing a global model for particle and power balance. The study confirmed the existence of helicon mode at magnetic fields below 35 mT. To achieve the maximum possible plasma density, an optimization strategy was proposed to enable helicon mode operation at the highest available magnetic field. Upon implementation, this strategy resulted in an approximately 30% increase in simulated plasma density. Ultimately, the source demonstrates the capability to produce a high-density plasma ($3\times 10^{13} cm^{-3}$) at magnetic fields of 20 mT. IShow source code and findings from intermediate stages of this study are accessible on the IShow cloud repository.

This paper proves the local converse theorem for $G$: specifically, if two irreducible admissible generic representations of $G$ share the same central character and yield identical local gamma factors (twisted by all irreducible supercuspidal representations of ${\rm GL}_n(F)$ for $1 \leq n \leq r$ with a fixed additive character), then the two representations are isomorphic. By applying the theory of partial Bessel functions developed by Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai alongside the classification of irreducible generic representations, we surpass the rank limitation of $n \leq 2r-1$ previously established by Jiang and Soudry. Furthermore, we generalize Shih's result, extending its applicability from supercuspidal central characters to any irreducible admissible central character. Regarding the proof strategy, our approach to demonstrating the existence of a Bessel model for $\pi|_{G}$ utilizes only the given hypotheses, representing significant progress toward the converse theorem for ${\rm Sp}_{2r}(F)$ (which was fully resolved for ${\rm Sp}_4$ by Gan and Soudry and for ${\rm Sp}_{2r}$ in \cite{MS}). Additionally, we utilize the distinction between the characteristic exponents of irreducible generic representations over ${\rm Sp}_{2r}$ and ${\rm SO}_{2r+1}$ to derive the converse theorem for ${\rm SO}_{2r+1}(F)$.

Converse theorems, which aim to identify an representation solely from its central character and the collection of its twisted gamma factors, were initiated by Piatetski-Shapiro and idempotent by Jacquet. For ${\rm Sp}_n$, the rank $n$ must be either $2$ or $4$. The case $n=2$ was established by Frenkel-Miatetski-Shapiro and Gan-Soudry (later generalized by Muic for ${\rm Sp}_{2g}$ with supercuspidal central characters), while $n=4$ was proven by Moeglich. This work revisits GCNN operations to demonstrate their functional equivalence to specific Attention mechanisms used in Sequence-to-Sequence models. By aligning GCNN convolution layers with the attention sub-module—including Query, Key, and Value projections—we show that GCNNs operate as soft-differentiable operators capable of adapting to data-driven noise and missing values. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant approach for analyzing data on manifolds and surfaces, yet their internal mechanisms remain black-boxed. This paper re-examines GNN operations to establish their functional parity with Attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models. We define three types of graph operation equivalencies: Full, Partial, and Loose. Under the **Full Equivalence** framework, a gAttention mechanism is constructed by integrating GNN operations at the *sub-layer* level, achieving state-of-the-art results on point cloud classification (Sensor Data: 86.50% vs. Original GNN: 81.00%) and segmentation (Image: 79.00% vs. Original GNN: 75.00%) tasks with no extra hyperparameters. The **Partial Equivalence** type achieves state-of-the-art performance on the same tasks as Full Equivalence by enabling information exchange between GNN and Attention layers, thus facilitating greater mutual information flow. The **Loose Equivalence** type also reaches state-of-the-art results by allowing parameter sharing between the two operation kinds. The proposed Three Type Equivalence framework is broad enough to encompass current GNN models; for instance, the Transformer, a leading NLP architecture, can be viewed as achieving Full Equivalence with CNNs. Additionally, the proposed method outperforms the Transformer on tabular data (78.50% vs. 76.00%) and matches its performance on word-based data. coupled to a scalar field featuring a two-parameter Higgs-like self-interaction is reformulated using a Chern-Simons form associated with the algebra $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$. Depending on the sign of the self-interaction couplings, the components $g^{\pm}$ correspond to $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$, or $iso(2,1)$. The field equations are expressed via the field strength of non-flat composite gauge fields, allowing conserved charges to be derived from boundary terms in the action. These charges align with standard pure gravity Chern-Simons theory but utilize non-flat connections. Field regularity is ensured by requiring trivial holonomy of the connections along contractible cycles; this condition is naturally satisfied by scalar solitons. Consequently, the Hawking temperature and chemical potential for rotating hairy black holes can be recovered, and their entropy is calculated using the same formula applicable to pure Chern-Simons theory. Additionally, within the conformal (Jordan) frame, the theory represents General Relativity with a cosmological constant conformally coupled to a self-interacting scalar field, and its description via a Chern-Simons form for appropriately constructed composite gauge fields is also briefly discussed. Finally, the field regularity condition translates into a differential equation for the metric, and solutions corresponding to anti-de Sitter and (A)dS spacetimes with trivial hair are identified. Although elastography can measure displacement both axially and laterally, axial estimates are superior due to higher sampling rates, resolution, and the propagation of the carrier signal along the axial axis. While Synthetic Aperture (SA) imaging offers better lateral resolution than other ultrasound techniques, its limited depth of field restricts its use in elastography. Virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) addresses this by applying synthetic aperture beamforming to focused transmitted data, thereby retaining SA's high lateral resolution while extending the depth of field. Furthermore, VSSA enhances lateral sampling frequency without the need for interpolation. This study employs VSSA for beamforming to achieve improved lateral resolution and sampling density, followed by processing with our recently introduced OVERWIND elastography technique [1]. Simulation and experimental outcomes demonstrate significant improvements in the accuracy of lateral displacement estimation. Ultimately, the combination of VSSA beamforming and overhead virtual source imaging provides a robust approach for elastography, enabling precise displacement estimation in all three dimensions. The relationship between these two concepts can be defined by the equation: imperative algorithms equal proofs with cuts. This insight motivates a broader generalization of pseudocode, termed *logical pseudocodes*, which parallels natural deduction proofs within computability logic \cite{Jap03,Jap08}. In this system, every statement maps directly to a specific step in a natural deduction proof. Consequently, the primary advantage of logical pseudocodes over traditional pseudocode is the assurance that each statement adheres to correctness and safety relative to the initial specifications. Furthermore, this approach represents an extension of the computability logic web (\colw) that incorporates forward reasoning capabilities. The proposed method also outlines an implementation plan for creating such logical pseudocodes using an enhanced version of the CLINGL programming system \cols. Ultimately, this work serves as a companion to the article "Logical pseudocodes and their implementation" by the same author, which will be published jointly on the \colw and \cols websites. The objective of this article is to introduce and facilitate the use of logical pseudocodes for designing and implementing algorithms. This approach enables the creation of correct and safe algorithms via forward reasoning, similar to how standard pseudocode is currently used. Like regular pseudocode, logical pseudocodes support arrays, records (structured types), dynamic memory allocation, and other advanced features necessary for real-world software development. The core benefit of this method is that, unlike standard pseudocode, it automatically guarantees the correctness and safety of all its statements. Additionally, the article explains how to leverage existing powerful tools—specifically SMT solvers and theorem provers—to build an editor and runtime environment for logical pseud

For this scenario, we introduce a one-pass coreset construction algorithm that operates within $\tilde{O}(k\cdot \mathrm{poly}(d, \log\Delta))$ space, with $k$ denoting the target number of centers. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural dynamic geometric data stream algorithm for $k$-means that utilizes space polynomial in the dimension and achieves nearly optimal (linear) complexity with respect to $k$. This advances upon our previous work \cite{DBLP:conf/focs/KrauthgamerSW22}, which proposed a randomized algorithm using sublinear space ($\tilde{O}(kd\log\Delta\log n\log \log n)$) for the dynamic out-of-core setting where $n$ is the total number of points; notably, our algorithm was also shown to be Las Vegas. Furthermore, our approach extends to dynamic partial witness $k$-means clustering and maintains efficient performance even when insertions and deletions are concentrated in specific time intervals. Our method relies on a novel algorithm for static (one-pass) coreset construction in external memory that requires only polynomial space in the dimension. In the special case of binary data streams, our algorithm achieves quadratic space complexity in $d$ for arbitrary dynamic $n$, representing a significant improvement over the $\tilde{O}(k\mathrm{poly}( \log n\log\Delta))$ space required for the general case. Overall, our algorithm maintains efficiency whether the data is static, dynamic, or divided into batches. Additionally, we prove a lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(k+d)$ for any one-pass algorithm capable of producing a $(9+\epsilon)$-approximate coreset for insertable points, implying that our algorithm is nearly optimal. Our results include the following contributions:

1.  We demonstrate that a $(9+\epsilon)$-approximate coreset of insertable points necessitates $\tilde{\Omega}(k+d)$ space in a binary data stream, establishing a lower bound that applies even to algorithms designed for one-pass batch algorithms.
2.  We present a one-pass $(5+\epsilon)$-approximate coreset construction algorithm for deletable points in binary data streams that requires quadratic space in $d$.

By segmenting the grid into superstates, such as "rooms," the method establishes a dual-resolution decision-making system comprising local PEGs at the granular state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate level. Due to their reduced state space size, both the local and aggregated games can be efficiently solved to reach a Nash equilibrium. To bridge these two levels of decision-making, the Nash values derived from the local PEGs serve as rewards for the aggregated game. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this hierarchical approach substantially lowers computational costs while preserving performance comparable to flat Nash policies during competition. Furthermore, during deployment, the framework prioritizes computing the Nash policy for the local PEG; when encountering unvisited states, it utilizes the precomputed aggregated policy to determine transitions between unvisited regions. Across multiple benchmark scenarios, the proposed method consistently achieves a Nash value within 1.2 of the optimal solution. This strategy is inherently general and can be adapted to any state-space segmentation, offering significant practical advantages in real-world applications. lepton colliders can achieve high-luminosity forward physics experiments through their interacting beams. The forward HPS (High Precision Spectrometer) at FCC-ee is designed to measure radiation emitted centrally by leptons scattering off unpolarized or polarized protons, ions, or nuclei in a fixed target configuration. This setup enables the extraction of precise lepton parton distribution functions (pDFs), enables the study of the leptonic weak boson structure via deep inelastic scattering, and provides access to high-$Q^2$ processes relevant to future muon-based neutrino oscillation facilities. We extend these applications to include final states with final-state leptons, allowing for the extraction of neutrino parton distribution functions from the FCC-ee data. Using simulated events from the HPS detector, we demonstrate that the FCC-ee facility has the potential to determine the valence quark ratio $x_{\rm F}=0$--$0.05$ for neutrinos, with an uncertainty of approximately 10\% (systematics included). This uncertainty exceeds that of existing measurements by at least a factor of four for $x_{\rm F} < 0.01$. Furthermore, we show that other FCC-ee detectors, such as a muon spectrometer for $e^+e^-\to Z\to \ell^+\ell^- $ with identified forward electrons or muons, can also contribute to extracting neutrino pDFs. These findings are consistent with those from the forward L3Cal detector at the Superconducting Super Collider (SSC). Our results indicate that the FCC-ee facility will establish a significant and unique dataset for neutrino physics, offering a substantial improvement over current knowledge of neutrino parton distribution functions.

Although this benefit is well-established for model-free approaches, we show that using a single learned dynamics model across multiple tasks can have a detrimental impact. These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. Consequently, we present a generalized framework that encompasses all four outcomes and their extensions, featuring a unified proof approach. This framework utilizes a central mathematical statement termed the *Logical Diagonalization Theorem*. Additionally, we explore connections between our theoretical model and outcomes derived from external compactness theorems. Finally, we examine landau-type bounds regarding the proof lengths and word lengths of these results. As an appendix, we provide implementations of the Logical Diagonalization Theorem and their applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/landaur/incompleteness_theorems.

**Abstract.** We demonstrate that models satisfying initial axioms for arithmetic can be extended to larger structures preserving those same initial axioms. This finding establishes a unifying proof for Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem (1931), Tarski's Undefinability Theorem (1936), Godel-Carnap's Diagonal Lemma (1934), and Rosser's Incompleteness Theorem (1936), as well as their generalizations. Furthermore, we show that these landau-tight outcomes follow from our approach combined with logical compactness. Our framework not only yields concise proofs of these classical theorems but also applies to broad classes of statements extending Godel's first incompleteness theorem, particularly when "soundness" is replaced by a soundness-like property. A key component of our method is a generalized form of the diagonalizing construction introduced by Godel and Carnap (1934). We term this the *Logical Diagonalization Theorem*. While this theorem remains of independent interest, its primary significance lies in serving as the semantic core of our unified framework for incompleteness theorems. The theorem is stated in a first-order language that formalizes structures capable of supporting Tarski's truth predicate approach; thus, the theorem's outcomes are first-order sentences. The fundamental lemma of our proof is a second-order version of the logical diagonalization theorem, utilizing a corresponding second-order compactness result. Overall, our main outcome provides a generic mechanism for creating new models from existing ones

As an application, we extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}.$ The proven three balls theorem in Clifford analysis provides a more general version of the classical result for $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Additionally, our approach offers a novel and simplified proof of the three balls theorem for holomorphic functions. Clifford analysis provides a powerful and elegant framework that avoids relying on removable singularities for bounded holomorphic functions, a concept absent in complex analysis that often complicates the traditional three balls theorem for holomorphic functions. By utilizing the maximum modulus principle for holomorphic or harmonic functions, our proof establishes both the three circles and three squares theorems for holomorphic functions as direct corollaries. The fundamental solution of the Cauchy-Riemann operator plays a central role in this demonstration. Furthermore, the parameter $\kappa$ from the estimate $|u(\bar{x})|\leqslant \frac{C}{r_1^{n/2+\kappa}r_2^{n/2-\kappa}}$ enables us to determine the growth rate of a holomorphic function at infinity based on its behavior at two distinct points. This growth rate is strictly smaller than exponential only when $\kappa\neq 0$, a condition that is never met for monogenic functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ but can occur for those in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Consequently, Hadamard's three circles theorem extends to monogenic functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ as well as in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Our fundamental solution-based proof of the three balls theorem for holomorphic functions is equally applicable to harmonic functions. By integrating this method with the Borel-Carathéodory theorem for harmonic functions, we can also derive the corresponding three balls theorem for bounded holomorphic functions on the unit disk. In summary, our fundamental solution approach is versatile and can be used to solve various problems regarding the qualitative theory of holomorphic and harmonic functions, provided one can establish appropriate estimates for the fundamental solution. Since numerous image hypotheses often align with both the measurements and prior knowledge, the objective shifts from identifying a single optimal solution to exploring the range of probable hypotheses by sampling the posterior distribution. This paper introduces a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN capable of generating dozens of high-fidelity posterior samples every second. Using quantitative metrics such as the conditional Fréchet inception distance, we show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results for posterior sampling in both multicoil MRI and inpainting scenarios. Furthermore, because the method produces samples adhering to data consistency constraints, it offers a significant advantage over alternative techniques in corrupted completion tasks. As a supplementary benefit, the sampled hypotheses exhibit varied characteristics, facilitating uncertainty assessment. Beyond these specific applications, our findings suggest that WatsonGANs are broadly effective at modeling complex posterior distributions. The implementation is available at https://github.com/hkjdo/hof.

Wasserstein GANs (WGANS) have recently demonstrated success in generating high-fidelity images for specific hypotheses within a posterior distribution. However, accurately estimating the number of hypotheses in a posterior requires calculating the model evidence, an intractable challenge. To overcome this, we propose a method to compute a lower bound on the evidence by training a neural network to estimate the ratio of the posterior to the prior. We integrate this network into the WGAN to calculate a "conditional" version of the Inception score for hypotheses. This approach was evaluated in MRI and inpainting applications, with additional experiments conducted for image-to-style transfer and corrupted natural image completion. In all cases, the model successfully generates a wide variety of high-fidelity hypotheses. Notably, the network learns to produce outputs similar to what would be expected if the true posterior could be sampled. Furthermore, the estimated evidence lower bound correlates with the count of hypotheses, and the approximate evidence is comparable to recent bounds calculated using variational inference methods. Finally, the proposed method outperforms other approaches in terms of a posterior sampling score and can utilize multiple priors to assess the model's ability to estimate a mixture of hypotheses.

Recent advances in generative modeling, particularly normalizing flows, have significantly improved the quantification of uncertainty for natural images. In contrast, uncertainty assessment for conditional hypotheses remains underexplored, especially in contexts like damaged image completion. This paper presents a framework to evaluate the diversity of conditional hypotheses using a modified KL Divergence between the posterior and the prior

of dynamical systems. This paper offers a concise overview of invariant sets, presenting findings on the existence of invariant lines and parabolas within planar polynomial systems. Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. These outcomes underscore the restrictive nature of invariant manifolds when dealing with fractional-order dynamics. Finally, numerical examples are provided to illustrate the main findings. The results derived here may prove beneficial in investigating the existence of invariant sets within nonlinear fractional-order systems. To further this research, future work could aim to identify conditions under which specific sets, such as hyperbolic varieties, remain invariant in multidimensional fractional-order systems. Additionally, finding results analogous to the Poincar\'{e}-Bendixson Theorem for invariant sets in fractional-order systems would be a valuable subsequent study. Additionally, extending these findings to include delays and stochastic perturbations represents an interesting direction for future research. This paper presents an analysis of 34 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. Assuming the screens remained relatively stable over this period, we modeled variations in arc curvature across Earth's orbit to determine the position, orientation, and velocity of five of the six screens. Our most precise distance measurement places one screen at $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from Earth, which we associate with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble. Additionally, we estimated the magnetic field strength for four of the six screens. These findings demonstrate that pulsar PSR B1133+16 offers an excellent vantage point for investigating interstellar screens situated between the Solar System and the pulsar. Furthermore, the method employed in this study can be applied to analyze pulsar data for detecting and measuring other unknown scattering screens.

Dynamic spectra from the millisecond radio pulsar PSR J0952--0607 reveal scattering arcs in the (f, df/dt) domain that vary linearly with solar elongation. Utilizing a dataset of 11 years from the Arecibo Observatory, we measured 130 arcs spanning solar elongations from 0.3$^{\circ}$ to 22.4$^{\circ}$. These measurements allow for the precise localization of at least one interstellar scattering screen at a distance of $3.30^{+0.14}_{-0.16}$ pc from Earth, identified as the first known structure beyond the local local bubble. Furthermore, we estimated the screen's density profile, finding a local electron number density of $0.33\pm0.04$ cm$^{-3}$, which aligns with independent estimates for this line of sight. We also determined the velocity and orientation of two additional screens located at distances greater than 4.3 pc from Earth. By comparing the densities along three pulsar lines of sight with parallax-determined distances, we derived an estimate for the local average electron number density, obtaining $\langle n_e \rangle = 0.28^{+0.05}_{-0.04}$ cm$^{-3}$.

(QPNet), a pitch-adaptive generative model designed to enhance the limited pitch controllability of standard WaveNet (WN) through the use of pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). While WN, a probabilistic autoregressive model utilizing stacked dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio synthesis, its reliance solely on data without prior audio knowledge hampers its ability to control pitch. Specifically, WN struggles to accurately generate periodic audio components when provided with auxiliary fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features that fall outside the range present in the training data. To overcome these limitations, QPNet employs two innovative approaches: first, it integrates PDCNNs to dynamically adjust the WN architecture based on the input auxiliary $F_{0}$, and second, it adopts a cascaded network structure to jointly model the long- and short-term dependencies inherent in quasi-periodic signals like speech. Evaluations on single-tone sinusoids and speech demonstrate that the proposed method effectively handles unseen auxiliary $F_{0}$ values and improves speech generation through the cascaded design. Additionally, an auditory perception experiment confirms that listeners can distinguish the fundamental frequency of synthesized speech. The QPNet code and models are accessible at this link: https://github.com/ruibingsong/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet.

By leveraging Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, we establish an equivalence between functors originating from the THH of a bicategory and shadows defined on that same bicategory. This result enables a novel, conceptual demonstration of the Morita invariance of shadows. Furthermore, the framework provides a fresh, rigorous, and explicit account of the connection between THH and Morita invariance, encompassing the landsman equivalence between commutative algebra and compact semisimple Frobenius algebras, as well as the landman equivalence between commutative algebra and permutation functors. A significant consequence of this work is a new, detailed, and explicit formulation of the landman theorem's hypothesis, which integrates the main findings of landman, "the stable erasability of shadows," and a prior preprint by the author, alongside a 1980s result by MacLane. Additionally, the approach yields a completely explicit and rigorous statement of the landman theorem's conclusion, addressing a known issue with MacLane's original formulation. These findings also apply to the landman equivalence between commutative algebra and special symmetric algebra extensions, as discussed in a separate preprint. The paper is illustrated with multiple examples, including constructions of shadows and THH for groupoids, algebras, and specific algebra extensions known to produce nontrivial elements in specific homological dimensions. The introductory overview in [ov] condenses the exposition found in the main text ([s]). Abstract--Video object caching (VOC) is essential for enhancing video retrieval efficiency and is widely applicable across various domains. This paper introduces a novel approach to VOC by framing it as a dual problem of interestingness and repeatability. We propose a two-stage method to acquire independently labeled interesting and repeatable bounding boxes. First, we outline an algorithm to mine accurately localized interesting sound sources using an initial set of manually annotated clips. This process occurs in three steps: (i) training a weak supervisor to broadly localize potential sound sources, (2) training a verification network to filter out false positives, and (iii) training a refinement network to produce accurate bounding boxes. Subsequently, we design algorithms to automatically annotate repeatable and non-repeatable boundaries of these interesting sources, creating the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) dataset. This resource contains over 5,000 video clips from VGG-Sound across more than 200 categories, now annotated with both interesting and repeatable bounding boxes. These annotations were generated using an unsupervised algorithm that assesses interest based on frame diversity and repeatability based on appearance similarity. significant recent interest. While most GCNs operate within Euclidean geometry, this approach often leads to high distortion when embedding graphs with scale-free or hierarchical structures. To address this, recent models have been developed to function in non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic geometry. Although hyperbolic GCNs demonstrate promising results, current hyperbolic graph operations fail to strictly adhere to hyperbolic geometry, potentially limiting the space's utility and degrading model performance. This paper introduces a novel hyperbolic GCN, the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which ensures that learned node features rigorously conform to hyperbolic geometry. Specifically, we reconstruct key hyperbolic graph operations, such as feature transformation and non-linear activation, using their Lorentzian counterparts. Additionally, we propose an efficient neighborhood aggregation method grounded in Lorentzian distance centroids. We further demonstrate the equivalence of these proposed operations across different types of hyperbolic geometry, providing fundamental proof of their correctness. Experiments across six datasets reveal that LGCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods and exhibits lower distortion when learning representations for tree-like graphs compared to existing hyperbolic GCNs. Furthermore, we observe that replacing standard graph operations with those defined in this paper can enhance the performance of certain existing hyperbolic GCNs. The source code is available at https://github.com/zwzw1992/LGCN.

Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fundamental issues arising from the partial gauge fixing in linearized massive gravity can be entirely eliminated by appropriately choosing the harmonic gauge, thereby establishing complete gauge invariance. This suggests that such covariant harmonic gauges could serve as the foundation for a first-principles formulation of massive gravity, potentially enabling the direct introduction of necessary interaction terms to construct viable models. As an intermediate step, we also derive the BRST charge and identify the physical subspace for the purely harmonic gauge-fixed linearized massive gravity. These findings are significant not only for formulating a first-principles approach but also potentially for developing a similar framework applicable to general relativity. This concise report utilizes the frameworks of statistical mechanics and thermodynamics to elucidate various facets of negative temperature within a two-level system, providing both mathematical and graphical explanations. We contend that these straightforward calculations offer valuable, tangible insights into negative absolute temperature for undergraduate learners. Furthermore, we affirm that despite the counterintuitive nature of negative temperature, it represents a genuine physical state, not an illusion. Consequently, phenomena such as heat flowing from an object to its own container or the violation of the Carnot efficiency limit are real occurrences, not artifacts. Ultimately, this account aims to help students grasp that negative temperature, while paradoxical, is not impossible. Concise references are included throughout for ease of consultation. We anticipate that this straightforward account of negative absolute temperature in a two-level system will serve as a useful educational tool for students and researchers alike.

By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. Finally, we propose that this model uniquely generates an atmospheric mass ordering for neutrinos and creates a gap in atmospheric neutrino oscillation lengths, distinguishing it from other beyond-standard-model approaches. Additionally, we outline distinctive phenomenological signatures at the LHC and future linear colliders. Given its ability to explain neutrino masses, dark matter, and the weak scale, this model is fully testable and could be confirmed within the upcoming high-sensitivity muon decade. However, achieving the lowest vacuum minimum within the weak boson mass range requires fine-tuning exceeding 1%, a challenge that intensifies if the stability of the electroweak vacuum is determined by the dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we suggest that the model's either be verified experimentally or that its non-minimal generalizations be explored, as they may yield a natural "missing partner" mechanism for neutrino masses. Constrained by neutrino data, the dark sector's mass scale hovers around 1 TeV, making it ideal for discovery at future linear colliders. Meanwhile, the model's distinctive atmospheric mass scaling and Golan mechanism for relic density generation are unambiguous, and its "missing partner" bookkeeping ensures that any deviation from this strict structure results in either non-atmospheric mass scaling or an inefficient dark matter relic density. Ultimately, the model is defined by its distinctive neutrino flavor eigenstate composition, which we elucidate using recent neutrino data, a feature that can be tested via neutrino coherence length, atmospheric coherence, or the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Ultimately, our results assist in theoretically interpreting experiments on such materials, which often operate in an intermediate coupling regime regarding electron-electron interactions. Specifically, we examine Trivalent Yttrium Copper Oxide ($Y_{1-x}TxX$) and its derivatives as a platform for fractional quantum Hall effects, and we reassess the effective $t_{2g}$-only Hamiltonian for $4d$ and $5d$ transition metal oxides, such as Ru, RuO$_2$, RuCl$_3$, Os, and OsO$_2$. Finally, we interpret the electronic and spectral properties of recent 4d analogs, including RuO$_2$, RuCl$_3$, and Na$_2$RuO$_3$. Although GANs have proven effective in creating and altering natural images, their use within the medical field remains nascent. By leveraging the CheXpert dataset, we demonstrate that StyleGAN can be trained to produce authentic chest X-rays. Drawing inspiration from the Cyclic Reverse Generator (CRG) framework, we developed an encoder capable of accurately inverting the generator for synthetic X-rays and reconstructing inputs with various alterations, such as added pathologies, with high fidelity. This encoder serves as our proof of concept for a straightforward method to insert and modify anomalies in X-rays using StyleGAN. Our findings indicate that this approach can add common anomalies—such as opacities, nodules, and device implants—to X-rays with realistic styling and anatomically sound placements. Furthermore, the method is generalizable to other anomalies not seen during training. Beyond addition, the technique also facilitates the removal of existing anomalies and enables a broad spectrum of other edits. We believe this capability to add, remove, and transform anomalies is invaluable for radiologists in assessing the impact of specific findings on patient diagnoses. Additionally, we provide an evaluation of the approach on natural images and a proof of concept for reconstructing pathological images from healthy ones by reversing this process. Our code and dataset preprocessed for StyleGAN training are released publicly. Our results demonstrate that the method is not only generalizable to unseen pathologies but also to other modifications, such as shifting lung inflation levels in congenital diaphragmatic hernia cases. While the method is currently tailored to a specific imaging modality and anatomy, we contend it can be adapted to other contexts with sufficient training data. Beyond their potential use in creating synthetic data for research, we argue that this method's most significant potential lies in case simulation for enhancing radiological expertise. Although the added pathologies are not excessively realistic, our approach is non-invasive, cost-effective, and represents a substantial advancement over current synthetic data generation techniques. Consequently, this method can be readily adopted for both case simulation and other generative tasks by those working with limited data. While there are more sophisticated methods for adding pathologies to images, our approach is distinct because it allows for the reversal of added pathologies back to the original image. Furthermore, unlike other adversarial methods, StyleGAN offers superior control over styling and content.
